Introduction:
The average age at pubertal onset has declined throughout the last century [ 1 , 2 ]. As earlier pubertal onset can have major health implications in adolescence and adult life, we need to identify potential modifiable factors in order to prevent further decline [ 3 ]. The Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC) Puberty Cohort was established in 2012 with three distinct purposes: (i) to estimate the current age at puberty in a population-based sample, (ii) to identify the causes of earlier puberty based on the hypothesis that prenatal programming might affect pubertal development, and (iii) to identify the consequences of earlier puberty. The data collection ended in 2021 when all participants had turned 18 years of age.

The aim of this review is to gather and present the results obtained from the DNBC Puberty Cohort—the largest of its kind in the World to date—based on >10 years of research. The following aspects have been investigated as potential causes of earlier puberty: genetic predisposition and certain congenital malformations, maternal lifestyle and dietary factors in pregnancy, maternal diseases and medication use in pregnancy, prenatal exposure to potential endocrine disruptors, birth-related and postpartum factors, child health, and anthropometrics in addition to prenatal and early-life exposure to psychosocial factors.
Methods:
This review is based on published studies from the DNBC Puberty Cohort [ 4 ], nested within the DNBC [ 5 ]—an ongoing nationwide cohort of Danish women and their children. Recruitment into the DNBC took place from 1996 to 2002 at the women’s first antenatal visit at around gestational Week 8 at the general practitioner and ∼30% of all pregnant women in Denmark were included.

The women provided comprehensive information on health and health behavior at enrollment and in four computer-assisted telephone interviews scheduled during the pregnancy (gestational Weeks 16 and 32) and after the birth (6 and 18 months postpartum). In gestational Weeks 8 and 24, they provided blood samples for storage in the Danish National Biobank [ 5 ] and, in gestational Week 25, a subpopulation (72%) completed a validated, semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire (FFQ). Seven- and 11-year questionnaires on maternal and child health and health behaviors have also been mailed to all participants for completion.

The DNBC Puberty Cohort includes a sample of children born to mothers participating in the DNBC, who answered the first interview in the DNBC and had not withdrawn from the DNBC by May 2012. Children were eligible for invitation if they were singletons who were born alive from 2000 to 2003. Of 56 641 eligible children, 22 439 were sampled [ 6 ] and invited to answer web-based questionnaires on current pubertal development. In total, 15 819 children (8123 girls and 7696 boys) participated ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ), corresponding to a participation rate of 70%. The questionnaires were sent out every 6 months from when the children were 11.5 years old until they reached 18 years or full maturity, defined as Tanner genital and pubic-hair development Stage 5 in boys and Tanner breast and pubic-hair development Stage 5 in girls [ 7 , 8 ]. Additionally, data on current pubertal development were obtained as part of the 11-year questionnaire. From 2012 to 2021, 98 195 questionnaires [average: 6.2 questionnaires (range 1–15)] were completed and returned ( Supplementary Table S1 ).

### Exposures

Information on exposures was obtained from gestational blood samples, from the DNBC enrollment form, DNBC Interviews 1–4, the mid-pregnancy FFQ, the 7-year and 11-year DNBC follow-ups, and by using ICD-10 diagnostic codes through linkage with the Danish National Patient Register (DNPR) and the Danish Medical Birth Registry (DMBR) ( Table 1 ).

### Outcomes

The pubertal milestones obtained from the DNBC Puberty Cohort included Tanner Stages 1–5 (breast and pubic-hair development [ 7 ] in girls and genital and pubic-hair development [ 8 ] in boys) with a short description and illustrations of each Tanner stage ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ); age at menarche (in years and months) in girls; the age at first ejaculation (in years and months) and voice break (yes, partly, no) in boys; and acne (yes, no) and axillary hair development (yes, no) in girls and boys.

Interpreting findings in our etiological studies, we looked at patterns of associations across the different pubertal milestones, but we also obtained a combined estimate according to the specific exposure of interest by using Huber White robust variance estimation. This technique reduces the risk of Type 1 errors by combining the estimates for the various individual milestones. These estimates are presented in the figures of this manuscript.

### Covariates

In all studies from the DNBC Puberty Cohort, potential confounding factors were identified by using existing literature and directed acyclic graphs. Information on covariates was obtained from the DNBC or from the Danish registers ( Table 1 ).

### Statistical analysis

The duration, timing, tempo, and synchronicity of puberty have been described in two descriptive studies [ 1 , 9 ]. Risks of selection bias and information bias were assessed in two validation studies [ 10 , 11 ].

The statistical methods are described in detail in the Cohort Profile [ 4 ] and in the Supplementary text . As the children from the DNBC Puberty Cohort answered questions on current development every 6 months, the data on puberty were censored [ 4 ]. Therefore, all outcome data were analysed by using a regression model for normally distributed censored data fitted by maximum likelihood estimation, using the intreg package in Stata. Moreover, all analyses were fitted with inverse probability of sampling and selection weights [ 6 ].
Results:
### Descriptive studies

In girls, the onset of puberty (Tanner breast Stage 2) occurred at 10.5 years and age at menarche at 13.0 years. In boys, the onset of puberty (Tanner genital Stage 2) occurred at 11.1 years, voice break at 13.1 years, and first ejaculation at 13.4 years [ 1 ]. In girls, the mean duration of breast development (Tanner Stages 2–5) was 6.2 years and the mean tempo was 0.72 Tanner stages/year. In boys, the mean duration of genital development was 5.0 years and the mean tempo was 0.90 Tanner stages/year [ 9 ]. The mean age at menarche in girls was 3.6 (95% confidence interval 3.1, 4.2) months earlier than the mean age in their mothers [ 1 ], indicating that the age at menarche has significantly declined across one generation.

### Validation studies

Using information on an externally obtained marker of pubertal timing—the height difference in standard deviation (HD: SDS)—we found no association between pubertal timing and participation in the DNBC Puberty Cohort. This indicates that participation was at most only associated with the exposure of interest, indicating a minimal risk of selection bias [ 10 ].

By performing clinical examinations of 197 participants and comparing those to the self-reported information obtained from the puberty questionnaires, we found that the self-assessment of the pubertal milestones was fair to moderate with no tendency towards under- or overestimation except for genital development in boys. No difference in self-assessment was observed across levels of socioeconomic status [ 11 ].

### Etiological studies

The results are presented in Figs 1 and 2 .

Girls and boys of mothers who reported earlier age at menarche than their peers had earlier puberty by ∼4 and 2 months, respectively. Hence, this study provides epidemiologic support for shared genetic determinants of the timing of puberty in boys and girls [ 12 ]. Parental fecundity [ 13 ] and congenital heart disease were not associated with puberty [ 14 , 15 ]. Boys with hypospadias had later puberty by ∼2–3 months, whereas cryptorchidism was not associated with puberty ( Fig. 1a ) [ 15 ].

Maternal pre-pregnancy obesity was associated with earlier puberty by ∼3 months in girls and ∼1.5 months in boys [ 16 ]. Maternal heavy smoking (>10 cigarettes daily) in the first trimester was associated with earlier puberty by ∼3 months in girls and boys [ 6 ]. Alcohol intake was not strongly associated with puberty ( Fig. 1b ) [ 17 ].

Paternal age of >35 years at birth was associated with earlier puberty by ∼1 month in boys [ 18 ]. Prenatal exposure to father absence was associated with earlier puberty by ∼3 months in girls [ 19 ] and prenatal exposure to maternal stress in pregnancy was associated with earlier puberty by ≤2–3 months in girls and boys ( Fig. 1c ) [ 20 ].

No consistent associations were observed for either dietary intake of nitrate or nitrate from drinking water [ 21 ], intake of folate or vitamin D supplementations [ 22 , 23 ], whereas lower vitamin D levels predicted by using the season as an instrumental variable was associated with slightly earlier puberty in girls and boys ( Fig. 1d ) [ 24 ].

Gestational diabetes mellitus was associated with earlier puberty by 2.5 months in girls [ 25 ]. Girls of mothers with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) experienced earlier puberty by ∼3.5 months. When only adrenarche (pubarche, axillary hair and acne) was looked at, girls of mothers with PCOS experienced earlier puberty by on average 5.4 months [ 26 ]. Preeclampsia, eclampsia or Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzyme, and Low Platelet syndrome were associated with earlier puberty by ∼2 months in girls [ 27 ]. Maternal hyperthyroidism was associated with earlier puberty by ≤3 months in boys [ 28 ]. Maternal nausea in the first trimester was not associated with puberty [ 29 ], whereas maternal asthma in pregnancy was associated with earlier puberty by ∼1 month in boys ( Fig. 1e ) [ 30 ].

Maternal unintended intake of oral contraceptives in early pregnancy was associated with earlier puberty by ∼1–1.5 months in girls and boys [ 31 ]. Neither prenatal exposure to antibiotics [ 32 ], glucocorticoid treatment [ 33 ], nor nitrosatable drugs [ 34 ] were strongly associated with puberty. Intake of acetaminophen in pregnancy showed a tendency towards earlier puberty in girls by 1.5 months ( Fig. 1f ) [ 35 ]. Prenatal exposure to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) was associated with altered puberty, although the magnitude (range: –7 to +5 months) and pattern of association varied by sex, type of pubertal indicator, and specific PFAS. Moreover, only a small sample ( n = 1167) had PFAS measured in maternal blood samples, thus the confidence intervals were broad ( Fig. 1g ) [ 36 ].

Girls and boys of mothers being in the first pregnancy trimester during the winter half-year had earlier puberty by ≤1 month [ 24 ]. Delivery mode was not associated with puberty [ 37 ]. Girls experienced slightly earlier puberty per standard deviation lower placental Z-score [ 38 ]. Being born large for gestational age (birth weight >90th percentile for age and sex) was associated with later puberty by ∼2 months in girls but by ∼1 month in boys, whereas being small for gestational age (birth weight <10th percentile for age and sex) was associated with later puberty by ∼1 month in both sexes [ 39 ]. Absence of breast feeding was associated with later puberty by 4 months in boys ( Fig. 1h ) [ 40 ].

Having atopic dermatitis was not associated with puberty [ 41 ]. Childhood obesity was associated with later puberty by ∼5 months in girls and ∼3.5 months in boys [ 42 ]. Father absence in childhood was associated with later puberty by ≤2–3 months in girls and boys [ 19 ]. Girls and boys with no siblings had earlier puberty by ≤5–6 months, and girls and boys with half and/or stepsiblings had earlier puberty by ≤2 months [ 43 ]. Gender incongruence (i.e. a mismatch between one’s gender and the birth-assigned sex) was associated with later puberty by 2–3 months ( Fig. 1i ) [ 44 ].

Overall, some of the studied exposures were associated with later puberty, some exposures showed weak or no associations with puberty, while some of the studied exposures were associated with earlier puberty of a magnitude that is likely to have a clinical impact at the societal level. Most pronounced were the associations for child obesity, maternal smoking in pregnancy, most psychosocial exposures, absence of breastfeeding (in boys), and most maternal gestational diseases ( Fig. 2 ).
Discussion:
### Key results

The DNBC Puberty Cohort was established and the data collection successfully completed with a high participation rate and several consecutive questionnaires per participant. Data were analysed by using state-of-the-art statistical methods. The estimated age at puberty in this large population-based sample indicated a further decline and characteristics such as pubertal tempo, duration, and synchronicity were described for both sexes. The validity of the collected information on pubertal milestones was deemed sufficient in terms of potential information bias [ 11 ] and the risk of selection bias was investigated and found to be minimal [ 10 ]. Moreover, several etiological studies identified associations with earlier puberty and, for some factors, also later puberty.

### Strengths and limitations

Children participating in the DNBC Puberty Cohort had parents of higher socioeconomic status and their mothers were more likely to be of normal weight, nonsmoking in the first trimester, and older at delivery compared with mothers of nonparticipating children [ 10 ]. Reassuringly, we found no association between puberty (by using a register-based marker of puberty) and participation in the DNBC Puberty Cohort, indicating a minimal risk of selection bias, even if the studied exposures were associated with participation [ 10 ].

Information on puberty was obtained by self-report. This approach was chosen following the recommendations of an expert panel urging the need for large-scale studies on pubertal timing [ 2 ]. In comparison, inviting children for a clinical examination is costly and induces a larger risk of selection bias due to lower participation rates and risk of selective participation by specific subgroups. Though we risk misclassifications, the self-assessment was found to be fair to moderate and independent of levels of socioeconomic status [ 11 ]. Moreover, the longitudinal data collection of all pubertal milestones constitutes a major strength of the DNBC Puberty Cohort, limiting the risk of misclassifications due to recall. Altogether, the study demonstrated that the self-assessment of pubertal development serves as a reasonable and time-saving tool to obtain pubertal information in a large prospective setting.

Enriched by the unique and detailed information from multiple follow-up waves in the DNBC, we had excellent opportunities to investigate numerous exposures by using the high-quality longitudinal data and to sufficiently control for confounding to an unmatched extent in cohort studies of this size.

### Interpretation

A secular trend of earlier age at menarche during the last century is evident [ 45 ]. The primary driver of the early part of this decline has been attributed to better nutrition and living conditions [ 45 ]. We found that girls had menarche at a mean age of 13 years—almost 4 months earlier than their mothers [ 12 ], indicating that the age at menarche is continuing to decline. We also found that childhood obesity was associated with significantly earlier puberty, suggesting that the obesity epidemic may be a major driver of this continuing decline [ 42 ]. Further, maternal age at menarche was strongly associated with puberty in both girls and boys, indicating a strong genetic component of pubertal timing overlapping between genders [ 12 ].

We found that both prenatal and childhood biological and psychosocial exposures might affect puberty. Our findings thus support the hypothesis that prenatal programming might affect pubertal development [ 46 ]. Most of the studied factors were associated with earlier puberty and the different exposures in combination may potentially drive some of the observed secular trend towards earlier puberty. The strongest risk factors for early puberty were child obesity [ 42 ], maternal smoking in pregnancy [ 6 ], most psychosocial exposures [ 19 , 43 ], absence of breastfeeding (in boys) [ 40 ], and most maternal gestational diseases [ 25–28 ]. This highlights the potential of intervening in e.g. maternal smoking in pregnancy to prevent earlier puberty. On the other hand, psychosocial factors do not offer obvious opportunities for intervention. Still, society and healthcare workers should know and understand these associations with the potential to identify vulnerable adolescents at an increased risk of earlier puberty.

Besides having no siblings, an absence of breastfeeding was the strongest risk factor for earlier puberty in boys, whereas breastfeeding was not associated with puberty in girls. On the contrary, most maternal diseases during pregnancy were associated with earlier puberty in girls, whereas boys appeared largely unaffected. Overall, maternal health and different exposures might influence puberty in a sex- and condition-specific manner. In addition to the well-established potential consequences of maternal diseases during pregnancy, prevention and treatment are likewise important in relation to the future reproductive health of children.

Environmental endocrine disrupters (EDCs) have been suggested to play an important role in the declining pubertal age [ 47 ]. Studies from the DNBC Puberty Cohort did not support consistent effects of EDCs, although we cannot exclude moderate effects of some of the examined factors [ 36 ]. Future steps would be to examine the potential cocktail effect of constantly being exposed to multiple factors in our environment and, in recent years, several analytic approaches have been developed for this purpose [ 48 ]. Further, capturing the true exposure levels by combining self-reported information with biological measurement in addition to details on the specific timing of exposure, duration, and dosage are important for improvements in future studies.

The DNBC Puberty Cohort has been extended to identify potential causes of later puberty too, as later puberty may also be associated with mental health consequences and fecundity [ 3 ]. We found that boys with hypospadias [ 15 ] and boys of mothers with asthma [ 30 ] had later puberty by ∼1–3 months. Also, most maternal dietary factors (folate, vitamin D) in pregnancy were associated with slightly later puberty in boys [ 22 , 23 ]. Hence, most associations with earlier puberty were strongest in girls and later puberty was primarily found in boys. This is concerning, as earlier puberty in girls and later puberty in boys may have psychosocial and mental consequences in adolescence [ 49 ].

Leveraging the unique longitudinal design of the unique DNBC Puberty Cohort, key risk factors associated with earlier puberty have been identified, thereby significantly advancing the scientific understanding within this critical area of research. A subset of the DNBC Puberty Cohort has already been genotyped and ongoing efforts to genotype even more participants aim to enable the integration of genetic, environmental, and social data, providing deeper insights into the interplay between these aspects and puberty.

### Perspectives

The data collection in the DNBC Puberty Cohort is complete and the children who were followed through adolescence are now young adults. Therefore, the consequences of earlier puberty can be assessed. By using the rich data in the Danish registries, all participants from the DNBC Puberty Cohort can be followed regarding the development of health conditions, morbidities, and medicine use. Further, in an 18-year DNBC follow-up, adolescents answered questions on mental health in a web-based questionnaire, enabling us to investigate associations between earlier puberty and self-reported mental health. During their twenties, they are invited to answer questions on health and health behavior, mental health and well-being, fertility intentions, and fecundity. This gives the opportunity to investigate whether earlier puberty is an early marker on the path towards poor reproductive health and health in general.
